articles.summary: Encontrou reuniu Lorenzo Pazolini (Republicanos) e Ricardo Ferraço (MDB) e foi mediado pela jornalista Rafaela Marquezini.
articles.body:
A TV Gazeta promoveu nesta quinta-feira (22) um debate entre os candidatos que disputam no segundo turno o governo do Espírito Santo . O encontro reuniu os candidatos para discutir propostas para o estado e confrontar ideias sobre temas como segurança pública, saúde, educação e transportes (assista a íntegra do debate no vídeo acima).

Participaram do debate, por ordem alfabética:

"Capixabas, muito obrigado por vocês todos que ficaram até essa hora acompanhando e podendo fazer uma comparação sobre esses dois projetos. Procurem rever amanhã esse debate e vejam se vocês encontram alguma coisa de concreto e de real no candidato. Eu chamei várias vezes o candidato para que ele pudesse olhar no fundo dos meus olhos e ele não faz isso. Só olha no olho do outro quem gera confiança. O que nós precisamos é isso.

São dois projetos, um projeto de continuidade, de aperfeiçoamento, de avanço, com experiência. O outro projeto é um projeto de ruptura, é um projeto que não dialoga com a vida real. É um projeto que até é muito simpático nas redes sociais, mas governar, liderar é muito mais que ser simpático nas redes sociais. É trabalhar, é ter capacidade de gestão, de transformação na vida das pessoas.

A mudança real é a continuidade com avanço e com velocidade e é isso que nós estamos experimentando no Espírito Santo. Esse é o meu compromisso com as famílias capixabas. Esse é o meu compromisso com as mulheres, com o respeito que eu tenho pelas mulheres, pelos jovens e pelos idosos. No dia da eleição, no domingo, com a sua escolha, você vai decidir o futuro do Espírito Santo. E o futuro tem nome, é Ricardo, é 15. Muito obrigado, capixabas."

"Olha, Rafaela, eu quero parabenizá-la pela mediação, parabenizar o candidato pela participação. Agradecer a você que já está nessa sexta-feira conosco. Agradecer a todos os capixabas que nos deram uma oportunidade única, um neto de taxista e de uma costureira, chegar ao segundo turno desse debate e principalmente ao segundo turno de uma eleição tão difícil.

Quero aqui agradecer a cada abraço, a cada olhar, a cada energia positiva. Foram dias, noites, madrugadas, debaixo de sol, debaixo de chuva, numa jornada que tem como objetivo cuidar da vida dos capixabas. E é essa história que nós vamos escrever a partir do ano que vem. Um novo tempo de harmonia, de amor, de diálogo, de compaixão e principalmente de formas de mudança da sua realidade social. Você se acostumará a ter um governador que estará nas áreas de vulnerabilidade social, estará nas áreas elevadas, no morro, na comunidade, assim como nós fizemos na nossa querida e amada capital. E é essa transformação que eu quero iniciar com você e é a partir de agora, no próximo dia 25, no próximo domingo. Eu quero contar muito com você para poder olhar nos seus olhos, para conectar os nossos corações e para isso eu preciso da sua confiança.

Dê essa confiança a alguém que se qualificou, que com muita fé e humildade chegou a esse momento do segundo turno. E eu quero pedir com muita humildade e olhando no fundo dos seus olhos o voto 10. Pazolini, o seu governador, por mais saúde, segurança, empatia e políticas públicas que transformarão a sua vida, 10."

articles.title: Brasileira diz não ver saída para recuperar filho levado há 4 anos ao Egito e pensa em desistir: 'Não consegui nada' | G1
articles.standfirst: Mesmo após conquistar a guarda no país africano, Karin Toledo afirma que esgotou as alternativas para reencontrar Adam, de quem não tem notícias diretas desde 2022.
articles.summary: Mesmo após conquistar a guarda no país africano, Karin Toledo afirma que esgotou as alternativas para reencontrar Adam, de quem não tem notícias diretas desde 2022.
articles.body:
"Eu tentei de tudo, eu fiz de tudo e eu consegui tudo. E, no fundo, eu não consegui nada" , afirmou a brasileira Karin Rachel Aranha Toledo sobre as tentativas de recuperar o filho, Adam, levado ao Egito pelo pai sem a autorização dela há 4 anos.

Após quatro anos de disputas judiciais, mudanças de país, decisões favoráveis nos dois países e tentativas frustradas de localizar a criança, Karin disse ao g1 que vive uma mistura de exaustão e impotência, e que não consegue enxergar quais caminhos ainda restam para recuperar o menino.

"Eu estou há quatro anos nisso e hoje eu não consigo enxergar uma saída para ter meu filho de volta", lamentou.

Imagem de arquivo de Adam, levado ao Egito em setembro de 2022 pelo pai sem autorização da mãe. — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

🔎 O caso começou em setembro de 2022, quando o pai levou o menino, então com 4 anos, do Brasil para o Egito . Desde então, Karin não voltou a ver o filho e passou a travar uma disputa internacional para tentar reavê-lo.

➡ No Brasil, a Justiça Federal de Campinas (SP) determinou a prisão preventiva do pai em 2023 e ele foi incluído na lista de procurados da Interpol . Karin se mudou para o Egito para acompanhar o processo e, em novembro de 2025, a Justiça egípcia concedeu a guarda do menino à mãe .

A Justiça egípcia também chegou a determinar a prisão do pai e da avó paterna por sete dias pelo descumprimento da ordem , e a defesa de Karin solicitou o aumento da pena para seis meses. Foram feitas ao menos três tentativas de cumprimento da decisão judicial para localizar Adam, sem sucesso.

Em junho, Karin contou que foi levada por uma instituição para a Bélgica após receber ameaças . De volta ao Brasil, atualmente ela afirma que não se sente segura para voltar ao Egito sem apoio.

"Eu não tenho condições de ir para o Egito e passar o perigo que eu passei da última vez, sozinha. Eu sou sozinha, sou eu por eu mesma. Não vejo nenhum tipo de saída, a não ser esperar o tempo passar e pedir a Deus para que, um dia, ele possa dar a oportunidade do meu filho poder me ver novamente ", disse.

A brasileira Karin Rachel Aranha Toledo, de Campinas (SP), tenta reaver o filho, Adam, que foi levado sem autorização pelo pai ao Egito desde 2022. — Foto: Bárbara Camilott/g1 | Reprodução/Redes sociais

Para Karin, a passagem do tempo é o aspecto mais doloroso da separação. "Mês que vem o Adam faz oito anos. Quatro anos não são quatro dias, são quatro anos perdidos ", desabafou.

Segundo ela, a distância fez com que perdesse referências básicas sobre a vida do filho. "Eu não sei o número que meu filho veste, o número que meu filho calça, o desenho favorito dele, o que ele gosta de comer. É como se a minha maternidade tivesse sido arrancada ", relatou.

A brasileira teme que o filho cresça sem saber dos esforços para reencontrá-lo ao longo dos anos: "Eu espero que um dia o Adam saiba que ele tem mãe. E que ele teve uma mãe que lutou a todo momento para estar com ele".

Além do impacto emocional, Karin calcula ter gasto mais de R$ 500 mil com as tentativas de recuperar o filho. O valor inclui despesas com advogados, deslocamentos e procedimentos necessários para acompanhar os processos judiciais.

O g1 procurou o Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública, a Autoridade Central Administrativa Federal (Acaf) e o governo do Egito, mas não obteve resposta até a publicação desta reportagem.

A Acaf é o órgão responsável, no Brasil, por adotar providências relacionadas ao cumprimento de acordos internacionais voltados à subtração internacional de crianças, à restituição internacional de menores e à adoção internacional.

O Ministério das Relações Exteriores informou que acompanha o caso desde 2022, por meio da Embaixada do Brasil no Cairo. Segundo a pasta, a representação diplomática presta assistência consular à criança e à família, incluindo interlocução com autoridades locais, visitas consulares, orientação jurídica e facilitação de apoio psicológico. Leia na íntegra abaixo.

"O Ministério das Relações Exteriores, por intermédio da Embaixada do Brasil no Cairo, acompanha o caso desde que foi notificado a respeito, em 2022. A Embaixada presta assistência consular ao menor nacional e a sua família - inclusive sob a forma de auxílio na interlocução com as autoridades locais, visitas consulares, aconselhamento jurídico e facilitação de apoio psicológico - e permanece em contato com as autoridades egípcias.

A atuação do Itamaraty no caso envolveu conversas de alto nível mantidas pelo Embaixador do Brasil no Cairo, Paulino de Carvalho, e pelo próprio Ministro Mauro Vieira com sua contraparte local.

A atuação consular do Brasil pauta-se pela legislação internacional e nacional. Para conhecer as atribuições das repartições consulares do Brasil, recomenda-se consulta à seguinte seção do Portal Consular do Itamaraty:

Em atendimento ao direito à privacidade e em observância ao disposto na Lei de Acesso à Informação e no decreto 7.724/2012, o Ministério das Relações Exteriores não divulga informações pessoais de cidadãos que requisitam serviços consulares e tampouco fornece detalhes sobre a assistência prestada a brasileiros."

articles.title: Thousands protest across Poland for access to free and legal abortions
articles.summary: Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.
articles.body:
Thousands of people have protested in more than 20 towns and cities across Poland, calling for access to free and legal abortion services.

Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.

Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government promised to liberalise abortion laws ahead of its 2023 election victory, but divisions within the coalition have slowed progress.

The demonstrations come days after parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions in the mostly Catholic country, but are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s conservative President Karol Nawrocki.

Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.

She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stand no chance of withstanding Nawrocki’s veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women’s support to win elections next year.

In the capital, Warsaw, about 1,000 protesters demonstrated in front of parliament despite rain.

“Over the last six years, nothing has really changed,” said 36-year-old Emilia Niemiec, who manages the AboTak abortion centre, which provides women with access to resources, including pills, and a space to be able to seek support or carry out a pharmacological abortion.

Restrictive abortion laws have been in place in Poland since 1993, with Polish women leading calls for the legalisation of abortion ever since. In 2016, nationwide demonstrations took place, with women donning black as a sign of protest.

But rather than being relaxed, Poland’s abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of foetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, with the overwhelming majority carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.

Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared with 452 in the whole of 2022 before Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.

Campaigners organising Thursday’s protests are claiming the Tusk government has betrayed Polish women – and that Tusk’s claims that women’s access to abortion has improved during his administration have actually complicated getting care for some women.

“The government’s promises act as a type of disinformation,” Marcinek said. “Women getting pregnant hear the prime minister say that everything is OK, that there is access to abortion, and then they end up in the hospital and see that is not the case. So they come to us when it’s very late and very complicated and expensive to help them.”

Two young women demonstrate with placards reading ‘How much longer do we have to wait?’ as they attend a nationwide pro-abortion rights protest [Mladen Antonov/AFP]

articles.title: Trump backs Ramaswamy ad featuring rival Amy Acton’s estranged mother
articles.summary: Trump advises the Republican gubernatorial candidate to keep running the controversial advertisement.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy amid controversy over an attack advertisement by the Ohio gubernatorial candidate against his Democratic rival.

Trump said in a social media post on Thursday that Ramaswamy should keep running the advertisement that features Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s estranged mother.

In the advertisement, Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, disputes her daughter’s account of a childhood involving homelessness and ⁠⁠sexual abuse by her stepfather, urging Ohioans not to vote for her.

Acton says she has not seen her mother since 1978. Acton’s brother has supported her account of being sexually abused by her stepfather when she was a child. The stepfather, who died in 2004, was charged with rape.

“Anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in office,” Trump said.

The US president also attacked Republican Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, who advised Ramaswamy to take down the advertisement, labelling him “disloyal” to the Republican party.

At a gathering with reporters at the Ohio Statehouse, DeWine recalled the painful experiences of rape victims he dealt with as a county prosecutor and state attorney general.

“It’s wrong to run this ad,” he said. “And, even at this late time – my wife, Fran, saw the advertisement just run this morning on TV – I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.”

Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, called the advertisement ⁠⁠a “desperate, disgusting attack”, while Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock called Ramaswamy’s decision to promote it “both despicable and entirely predictable”.

Vice President JD Vance, campaigning on Wednesday with Ramaswamy ⁠⁠and US Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican, had brushed aside ⁠⁠the blowback.

Vance, a former senator from Ohio, expressed disgust with Republicans “whining” about the advertisement as low and in poor taste.

Ramaswamy’s campaign said it was spending $4m to promote the advertisement.

Opinion polls suggest Acton is narrowly leading Ramaswamy in a tight race to replace the term-limited DeWine.

articles.title: N.Y. AG James files opposition to effort to bar her from Cornell investigation
articles.summary: One of the men named in an explosive lawsuit alleging sexual assault at a Cornell fraternity house opposed Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor.
articles.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James filed a response Thursday opposing an effort to bar her from acting as special prosecutor in the Cornell University rape investigation over claims of political bias. James said in a court filing that the petition to remove her as special prosecutor relies on claims that “are not justiciable.” An attorney for Gillio Lopes, one of seven men sued over allegations that a woman was raped at a Cornell fraternity house, filed a petition this month arguing that James “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt.” James wrote in the response that there is no standing, that even if there were the court should reject it and that the governor has the power to appoint a special prosecutor. “Petitioner asks this Court to impermissibly void a discretionary action by the Governor,” James wrote in the filing opposing the petition filed by Lopes’ attorney. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, appointed James as special prosecutor in the investigation of the Cornell case on Oct. 1. Hochul cited concerns about how university police and the local district attorney’s office handled the woman’s allegations of sexual assault in 2024. The woman alleged in a lawsuit that she was raped and plied with drugs at the fraternity house in 2024. The allegations have caused outrage, including fury about messages in a group chat about her on the night she alleges she was assaulted. No criminal charges have been filed. The lawsuit identifies the woman as Jane Doe. Attorneys for another former fraternity member named in the suit, Winston Lee, also filed a motion this month seeking to disqualify James from any future grand jury proceedings. That matter is pending. A spokesperson for James’ office said Thursday that it has not formally responded to Lee’s filing. Attorneys for Lee and Lopes have said their clients deny the accusations. Both Lee’s and Lopes’ motions argue bias by pointing to a post on the New York attorney general’s Facebook account on Sept. 28, before James was appointed special prosecutor. “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers,” it read. “To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.” In response to calls for James to step down from the role, she said this month that she was “committed to leading a comprehensive investigation they can trust, guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.”

articles.title: A California family spent about $4,000 and more than 200 hours turning its front yard into Jurassic Park, building 13-foot gates and a dinosaur escape show that visitors can watch for free
articles.summary: A family in Granada Hills, California, has spent about $4,000 (£3,080) and more than 200 hours building a huge Jurassic Park display in their front yard.
articles.body: A family in Granada Hills, California, has spent about $4,000 (£3,080) and more than 200 hours building a huge Jurassic Park display in their front yard. The attraction features 13-foot entrance gates and a timed dinosaur escape show that is free for the public to watch. Rob and Kel Warner turned their suburban property into a detailed tribute to the 1993 Steven Spielberg film. According to an exclusive report by People magazine, the couple built tall wooden entrance gates that stand higher than their single-storey home. The gates serve as the main entrance for neighbourhood trick-or-treaters and visiting fans of the film. The display includes custom-made moving dinosaur models, themed lighting, artificial fog, music from the film, and several life-sized dinosaur figures spread across the lawn.Custom gates and mechanicsThe project took months of hard work, planning, and testing. According to details the family shared with People magazine, they spent around $4,000 in total. This covered raw timber, the internal frames, special electronic controllers, and strong weatherproofing materials to protect the display from the elements. To recreate the film's famous entrance, Rob Warner designed and built wooden pillars and hanging gates that stand 13 feet tall. The structure needed reinforced ground anchors to support its weight and keep the gates steady during strong winds. Behind the gates, the front lawn features fake electric fencing, emergency warning lights, and tropical plants. These details are designed to recreate Isla Nublar, the fictional island resort and research centre in the film.Automated dinosaur escape showThe main attraction is a regular automated show that recreates a dinosaur escape. Visitors gather along the pavement to watch a planned light and sound performance. Warning sirens flash and beep, red emergency lights brighten the lawn, and life-sized dinosaurs appear to break free from their enclosures. The show uses audio and visual equipment hidden in the garden. Custom timers and relays control the sequence. They switch floodlights on and off, play recorded dialogue from the film, and trigger mechanical movements in the dinosaur models. This allows the show to run without the owners having to operate everything by hand. Kel Warner shares themed design projects and family outings on social media under the name @themeparkmomlife. She told People magazine that the family wanted to give local residents an immersive theme park experience without charging an entrance fee.Community reception and family traditionThe family began planning the project early in the year, with construction picking up over several months. Together, they spent more than 200 hours designing, building, and testing the mechanical features. Most of the work took place in the evenings and at weekends around their regular schedules. For the Warner family, creating large seasonal displays has become an annual community tradition. Neighbours and local visitors often stop by throughout October to take photos of the setup. The family also puts crowd control measures in place along the street during the busiest evening hours. Despite the time and money they have invested, the family allows visitors to enjoy the entire outdoor display for free. articles.title: Utah man charged with attempted hate crime after alleged threat to 'blow up' synagogue
articles.summary: A Utah man allegedly threatened to blow up a synagogue, and a search of his home uncovered six improvised explosive pipe bombs and rifles, officials say.
articles.body: A Utah man is facing several charges, including attempting to commit a hate crime, after he allegedly threatened to "blow up" a synagogue. Skyler AJ Rose, 22, of Ogden, was indicted by a federal grand jury on Wednesday, on multiple federal charges, including possession of an unregistered destructive device, threatening to kill or injure people and destroy a building with an explosive, and attempting to commit a hate crime, among other offenses, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Utah. "There is no place for hate motivated violence—attempts or otherwise—in our communities. A place of worship should be a refuge of safety, not fear," U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak for the District of Utah said in a statement. "Thanks to the dedicated work of the FBI and the outstanding efforts of our local police partners, these alleged threats were identified and stopped before anyone was harmed. Let these charges serve as a clear warning: if you attack or attempt to attack a place of worship, you will face the full force of the federal government." On Dec. 23, 2025, Rose allegedly made multiple threatening posts on social media, according to court documents. PENNSYLVANIA MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING ISIS ATTACK ARRESTED WITH RIFLE AND 190 ROUNDS OF AMMUNITION: DOJ "I wanna blow up a synagogue," one of the posts read, according to prosecutors. An investigation was launched and authorities learned that the posts were made from an IP address tracing back to Rose's home. The FBI then contacted the Ogden City Police Department to assist, with a home visit where authorities said they confirmed the social media handle belonged to Rose. Investigators executed a search warrant and recovered six improvised explosive pipe bombs and one inert device, explosive precursors and components that officials say could be used to construct further improvised explosive pipe bombs, a black Samsung cellphone and two rifles with accompanying magazines and ammunition, prosecutors said. FLORIDA MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING MASS SHOOTING TARGETING JEWISH EMPLOYEES AT ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION A subsequent search of Rose’s cellphone revealed that Rose searched online for a synagogue near him in November 2025. "Today’s indictment stops in its tracks an alleged plan to carry out a violent attack on a synagogue," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division said in a statement. "The Department of Justice will take decisive action to protect American worshippers from violent threats, no matter where they occur." Special Agent in Charge Robert Bohls of the Salt Lake City FBI added that "no one should have to fear for their safety because of their faith." Thanks to the swift, seamless collaboration with our law enforcement partners, we were able to address the threat and protect lives from potential physical harm." The investigation also allegedly revealed evidence of child sexual abuse material on Rose's cellphone, including hundreds of cached images and screenshots depicting child sexual abuse material, according to prosecutors. Rose was also indicted on charges of receipt and possession of child pornography. Rose's initial appearance is scheduled for Oct. 23 in federal court in Salt Lake City.

articles.title: 'Lifting sanctions will make Putin stronger': Zelenskyy differs with Trump on Russia
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said his differences with US President Donald Trump are “not about personalities”, warning that lifting
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said his differences with US President Donald Trump are “not about personalities”, warning that lifting sanctions against Russia would strengthen President Vladimir Putin and undermine efforts to end the war.In an interview with CNN in Kyiv on Thursday, Zelenskyy said he was opposed to easing sanctions on Moscow, arguing that Putin had no intention of ending the conflict.“My attitude to Putin is very clear. I think that if we lift sanctions, we will make him stronger. It’s not something personal between me and President Trump, and of course I’m against any lifting of sanctions.”Relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated in recent weeks. Zelenskyy had criticised Trump as being “on the wrong side of history” after the US president announced a deal to buy Russian fuel, raising concerns over international efforts to isolate Moscow. Trump subsequently waived some sanctions against Russia, drawing criticism even from members of his own party.Ukraine also faced restrictions on access to Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, as questions grew over Washington's continued support for Kyiv.Zelenskyy's remarks came amid renewed diplomatic efforts by Trump's envoys to find a resolution to the four-and-a-half-year war.Zelenskyy questions Putin's commitment to peaceUS special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday for three hours. Witkoff had met Zelenskyy in Norway a day earlier and described Putin as a “humanitarian” over his decision to release 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard.Trump said on Wednesday that tighter sanctions against Russia could have prevented Hubbard's release and damaged efforts to reach a peace deal.“You could forget about him, you’d never see him again, he’d be back in jail for 25 years,” Trump said in response to a question from CNN's Kaitlan Collins.He also argued that imposing sanctions during negotiations could jeopardise an agreement.“When you’re close to a deal and you have delicate negotiations, you don’t put sanctions on.”Zelenskyy described his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo as productive but said he remained doubtful about Putin's willingness to end the war. Putin has agreed to talks in November but has provided few details about the proposed discussions.Also Read: Will back all meaningful efforts for Ukraine peace, PM Modi assures Poland's Tusk“Putin is playing, you know, he is a player,” Zelenskyy said.“It’s a pity because he plays with the lives of other people, and of course he doesn’t want (to stop the war). So what we want from our partners (is) not to give him a possibility to be stronger and break us.”Trump said on Wednesday that his administration was “the closest we’ve been” to settling the conflict. However, Russia launched hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukraine overnight.Moscow has also maintained its demands for territory. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that negotiations were largely focused on the future of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine, most of which is under Russian control.“The fight now is really concentrated on what happens in the remainder of Donbas,” Rubio said, adding that “there’s been some creative ideas that have been put out there about how to resolve that difference.”Zelenskyy indicated that Ukraine could consider freezing the current front lines as a way to stop the fighting and begin negotiations. However, he ruled out giving up territory that remains under Ukrainian control or recognising Russian-occupied areas as part of Russia.The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire could provide an opportunity to halt the bloodshed and hold further talks.“Our land is very important because it’s about people. It’s not about kilometers,” he said. “A lot of people died defending this land, defending our independence, our country.”“Nobody will recognize these territories, which are temporarily occupied, as Russian territories, and I think Russia understands it. It’s a pity if somebody doesn’t understand, but it’s up to them,” he added.Ukraine seeks clarity on Starlink access, more air defence missilesThere have been some signs of improving ties between Washington and Kyiv after Ukraine accused the US of limiting intelligence sharing on incoming Russian missiles, restricting vital Starlink services and delaying weapons supplies.Zelenskyy said earlier this week that intelligence sharing had resumed. However, he told CNN that access to Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade satellite communications service, had not been fully restored.Trump said on Thursday that Musk had restored Ukraine's access to the military-grade version of Starlink, although he declined to say whether he had personally asked the billionaire to do so.Some Ukrainian military units reported improved internet speeds after the reported restoration. However, a source familiar with the matter told CNN that the improvement was not universal and that access did not provide unlimited speeds.The source said the service was “clearly not enough to intercept jet powered drones.” Ukraine is awaiting further information and clarification from the US, the source added.Ukraine is also facing a critical shortage of interceptor missiles. Although its military receives warnings about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, it does not have enough weapons to intercept them.Finland announces €300 million support packageZelenskyy announced on Thursday that Finland would provide Ukraine with a fresh support package worth €300 million ($336 million). The two countries also agreed to deepen cooperation, including through greater Ukrainian use of Finland's satellite capabilities.“Thank you for your willingness to support our logistics and energy sectors—these are key targets for Russia right now, and having more locomotives, more energy equipment, and more resources to protect our energy infrastructure will truly make a difference,” Zelenskyy said at a joint press conference with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo.He also said Ukraine needed more support from its European allies, particularly in air defence, as the missiles supplied so far were insufficient to protect the country.Zelenskyy said Ukraine needed two key things from its partners: “Not to lift sanctions from Putin … (and) to give us better missiles.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Washington Post journalist says attack by Israeli West Bank settlers has only ‘strengthened’ her resolve
articles.summary: Heidi Levine, the Washington Post journalist brutally attacked by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank last week, said the terrifying ordeal has only strengthened her resolve to continue covering the plight of Palestinians.
articles.body: Heidi Levine, the Washington Post journalist brutally attacked by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank last week, said the terrifying ordeal has only strengthened her resolve to continue covering the plight of Palestinians. “What hurts me the most is I can now really understand what others have gone through, what Palestinian women, children, men have gone through,” she told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Thursday from Israel, where she’s recovering after being released from hospital the day before. “I’m an American, I work for the Washington Post, my story is getting a lot of attention around the world, everyone wants to talk to me – but I can’t imagine what it’s like for all the victims that have gone through the same ordeal and are living with the threat of this violence on a daily basis,” she added. “It actually has strengthened my commitment to continue working to try to make a difference.” Levine, a veteran photojournalist known for her work in the Middle East, was covering the annual olive harvest in the West Bank when she, a group of Palestinians, and other journalists came under attack. Violence in the West Bank has surged in recent years as settlements have expanded, often backed by Israeli forces; attacks on farmers and communities who rely on the olive harvest for their livelihoods now come on a daily basis. Initially, Levine said, the harvest began as planned. But then, peering through her telephoto camera lens, she noticed people gathering at a nearby hilltop. They seemed young, some wearing black masks; she could see religious garments and headwear like kippah and tzitzit that she said clearly identified them as Israeli settlers. Their numbers slowly grew to reach several dozen. They began lighting the olive trees on fire and moving closer. “Then all of a sudden, chaos broke out,” she said. “There was tear gas, there was gunfire. From what I understand, a man was shot; a Palestinian man was shot in the leg, and the settlers charged forward,” she said. “I was thrown to the ground … They just kept kicking me and hitting me with sticks, and it just kept going on and on. And then I actually thought, okay, maybe I’ll just play dead and pretend I’m dead, and they’ll stop and they’ll leave me alone.” Instead, her attackers started ripping her gear off her body – her camera bag, her lenses, her pouch containing her American passport, credit cards, documents and other items. Then they hauled her to her feet, in a moment that has sparked controversy and debate in the week since videos of her attack emerged. In a statement after the attack, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.” This, Levine says, was false. “No, they only stood me up because they couldn’t manage to get everything off my shoulders to rob me, including ripping off my gold necklace that my daughter gave me for my birthday,” she said. The attack finally halted when journalist Jasper Nathaniel and several others came to Levine’s aid – but the danger wasn’t over. Video footage from that moment shows her rescuers holding her up and trying to escape from the attackers, who continue to throw rocks as they give chase. “Run, run!” Levine’s rescuers can be heard shouting in a panic. “I can’t,” she responds weakly. They urge her again: “You have to, come on!” Speaking to Tapper on Thursday, she described it as “this biblical battle where the Palestinian men, a group of men went in front of me to protect us, me and my rescuers from being attacked again.” Without the Palestinians’ intervention, the whole group “would have been in the same situation as me.” Even with a flak jacket and helmet on, Levine sustained serious injuries, with a broken rib, a broken vertebra, and a severe finger injury that required surgery, said Nathaniel last week after visiting her in the hospital. When she spoke to CNN, her hand was still heavily bandaged. Her attack was widely condemned by foreign press, the White House, and some Israeli leaders including President Isaac Herzog. Netanyahu, however, tried to cast doubt on Levine’s attack and said that “serious questions remain.” Just one day after Levine’s assault, settlers attacked a group of European diplomats visiting the Palestinian Christian town of Taybeh, prompting further outcry from the international community. On Monday, Israeli police arrested at least 10 suspects for both attacks. But many Palestinian victims of similar attacks never see justice. Since the olive harvest began on September 27, Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented more than 530 incidents of “settler and soldier violence” – which, beyond outright attacks, also includes the looting of crops and livestock, and destruction of olive trees. More than a quarter of the violence “occurs in solders’ presence and under their protection,” said Yesh Din. There has been a dramatic expansion of illegal settler outposts across the West Bank since Netanyahu’s government formed in December 2022 – with more than a third approved by the government. With that expansion, settler violence has also spread into parts of the West Bank that had previously seen little or none. When asked if she blames Netanyahu and other far-right Israeli leaders like national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for her attack, Levine laughed humorlessly. “Well, you hear their rhetoric, right? You hear their speeches. I’ve documented their visits in the West Bank, so I think the answer is pretty obvious,” she said, warning that things will only worsen, and that authorities “don’t even know how to handle it.” “This has been going on for over four decades that I have been covering this region, but I’ve never seen this situation in the West Bank or the situation in Israel at the level that it is today.”

articles.title: Met detective raped by fellow officer says police handling 'like being raped all over again'
articles.summary: Linda Williams was attacked by David Carrick, who was jailed in 2023 for sexual offences against 12 women.
articles.body:
A Metropolitan Police detective, who was raped by a fellow officer, has told the BBC that Scotland Yard's handling of her case was "like being raped all over again".

Det Con Linda Williams was attacked in 2004 by PC David Carrick - a serial abuser jailed for life in 2023 for sexual offences against her and 11 other women.

Linda has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because of the attack and sought damages from the Met for failing to protect her from Carrick. The lengthy civil case left her feeling suicidal, she says.

The "worst thing", she says, was when lawyers acting for the Met commissioner challenged the severity of her PTSD on the basis that she had been raped only once.

The Met has told the BBC it "tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams' welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible".

"We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer," the force added. "Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable."

Linda, who has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak to the BBC, has settled her civil case and the Met has now paid her compensation without acceptance of liability.

In an unprecedented move for a serving officer, she is now calling publicly for Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley to resign. She believes he has failed to change police culture as promised and she still does not trust her own force to handle cases like hers.

When he took on the most important job in UK policing in 2022, Sir Mark pledged to change the Met. At the time, the force was viewed as being in crisis - following Sarah Everard's murder by a serving officer and other scandals including officers sharing photos of murdered sisters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman.

After Carrick was jailed in January 2023, Sir Mark praised the victims and said: "We have failed and I'm sorry. He should not have been a police officer."

Two months later, in an official report by Baroness Casey, the Met was described as a "boys' club", that was institutionally misogynistic and had failed women.

Linda contacted the BBC, after seeing Panorama's report last year into a hidden culture of misogyny and racism inside the Met .

Since reporting the rape by Carrick in 2021, Linda says it has been "horrific" and she would not report a rape to the Met today "because I don't trust the police and I don't think they deal with it correctly".

Carrick was brought to justice by Hertfordshire Police, which investigated the rape of Linda. She reported it to the force after seeing media coverage of the news that Carrick had been charged with raping another woman.

Linda was herself a rape investigation officer in the early 2000s.

"I supported victims through rape but didn't report myself. I think that says loads.

"I'm asking members of the public to report, and I'm there to support them, but I wouldn't do it myself and I didn't do it."

She says if a similar attack happened to her tomorrow, she would not report it to the Met, because she has "no faith" that the force would deal with it correctly.

Carrick raped her while she was on a three-month attachment with him in south London - miles from where she was normally based.

One night, Linda says, Carrick suggested she should stay at his home, so she did not have to drive far late at night only to return early the next morning.

When Linda told him no, she says Carrick replied: "It's what I do. I'm going to carry on."

She knew that if she fought back then Carrick was going to get violent, she says.

Afterwards, Linda says she "never told a soul".

She says she felt unable to report the rape then, or for years afterwards, because of the culture in the Met.

Reporting the rape "would have been the end of my career", she says, because Carrick would not have been charged and she would have been shunned.

"I would imagine that if Carrick had been arrested, he probably would have been interviewed and then no further action. So then mud sticks, doesn't it?

"Then I'd be the officer that alleges rape, and who's going to want to work with me?"

The "very sexist" culture she says she experienced included having her forehead stamped with the words "Property of the Met" and being locked in the boot of a police car for the duration of a shift.

Linda, now 60, says the mental and emotional impact of the rape has been vast.

She has led a lonely life, she says, focused primarily on her work and pets. She has not had a relationship with a man since the day she was attacked and says she has missed out on having a family.

"I still don't feel I could have any relationship," she adds.

She feels guilty at not having come forward earlier to report Carrick, she says.

Since his conviction, she says the Met's culture has not changed as much as it should have done.

"We've not moved on enough in the police to really give victims of domestic violence, sexual offences any [of the] support they really need."

Her PTSD after the attack is "90% down to the Met Police, 10% to Carrick", she says.

Linda brought a civil case against the Met seeking damages on the basis the force failed to protect her from him and that she felt she had been unable to report the rape.

During the four-year case, she says the Met's legal team questioned the severity of her PTSD diagnosis.

"I was horrified and shocked," she says, adding she was reduced to tears and felt she was being called a liar.

The Met team also suggested her PTSD could not be severe because she had been raped only once, she says.

"I don't know how many times you have to be raped to have severe PTSD," Linda says

The BBC has seen a document from the Met, sent to Linda, showing it stated that a key factor in assessing damages was that the "abuse itself was isolated to a single episode".

Linda's solicitor, Sophie Bullimore, of Penningtons Manches Cooper, says to see the rape "reduced down on paper to it being a single isolated event, when actually it has impacted every single aspect of her life, it just needs to be handled with more care".

If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line

Linda says Met lawyers used the fact that she was an exemplary officer, and continued to perform well at work, to suggest she had shown no signs of psychological trauma.

This fails to understand trauma, or how it manifests itself, she adds.

The Met document, sent to Linda, shows it argued that - for at least 15 years after she had been raped - the psychological harm she experienced was "not such as to significantly impact her on a day-to-day basis".

The Met's legal approach, says Linda, felt "like being raped all over again" - with the force controlling the process and deciding what she was worth.

The lawyers were acting on behalf of the commissioner, whom she therefore regards as being personally responsible.

At the time of Carrick's conviction, Sir Mark publicly apologised to the 12 victims. Linda says she waited a couple of months to see if he would get in touch with her directly.

When she did not hear anything, she emailed, telling him that as "a serving officer, one of his troops, maybe I thought he would come forward and speak to me".

He did then meet her, she says, and "said he was sorry". But the apology lacked detail, she says, so it "meant nothing".

The commissioner lacks empathy and is more concerned with public perception than supporting victims or officers, she tells the BBC.

"I would like him to resign. I don't think he's fit for the job.

"My colleagues have been really supportive and absolutely fantastic, but the support from higher management isn't there."

Sir Mark has "repeatedly acknowledged" that Linda has shown courage in speaking out about her experience to drive forward necessary change and, in now waiving her anonymity, to continue to do so, said the Met spokesperson.

The commissioner has "contacted DC Williams to ask whether she would be willing to meet again and further discuss these issues in person", they added.

"I'm speaking out now because I want to help other victims, whether they're police officers, police staff or members of the public.

"We can turn it around, but I don't think Mark Rowley can turn it around."

articles.title: Slade star Dave Hill honours Wolverhampton in debut solo album
articles.summary: Slade legend Dave Hill's first solo album celebrates Wolverhampton roots and personal stories.
articles.body:
Slade star Dave Hill is set to release his debut solo album, paying homage to some of his old haunts in Wolverhampton.

Named Dirty Foot Lane, the 10-track album was named after a road near his childhood home and not far from where he lives today.

He collaborated with Noddy Holder's son, Django Holder, on the project, his first since the break-up of the band behind hits such as Merry Xmas Everybody.

"It's got a lot of depth to it, every one of those tracks is a true story about someone close or someone I've lost," he told BBC Radio WM.

The album blends rock, blues and folk, capturing the energy of Hill's live-performance roots alongside his personal journey, including struggles with mental health and the impact of the Covid-19 lockdowns.

"When I started to write, I knew when something was good - it would almost make me cry," the 80-year-old added.

He continued: "I was talking to Noddy Holder, [who is] probably one of my best friends in life, and he encouraged me to write my own music.

"Wolverhampton was where I lived. [I remember] the council estate and the cinema and growing up in the days when Doris Day was in the charts. I loved her. I used to watch Flash Gordon at the cinema."

Hill also teamed up with American country music star John Berry for the album.

He also told BBC Radio WM that he has plans to release two further albums in the future.

articles.title: Dorset coast under flood warning as Storm Austen sweeps in
articles.summary: The warning covers the coast at Chiswell, where strong winds and large waves are causing flooding.
articles.body:
A stretch of the Dorset coast is under a flood warning as Storm Austen sweeps in.

The Environment Agency (EA) has issued the warning for the coast in the Chiswell area and closed the A354 Portland Beach Road and the Causeway after flooding and waves overtopped the road.

The EA said: "We are closely monitoring the situation and we have staff on site" and urged people to avoid seafronts and harbours due to wave overtopping and spray containing debris.

The area under the flood warning also covers Brandy Row, Pebble Lane, Victoria Square up to the junction with Queens Road and the car parks along the A354 and the yard along Lerret Road.

Elsewhere trains are also disrupted between Poole and Bournemouth after a tree came down on the railway line near Bournemouth.

South Western Railway said train services running through these stations may be cancelled, delayed by up to 60 minutes or revised. Disruption is expected until midday.

The rail firm said replacement buses were set to run between Bournemouth and Brockenhurst.

A flood warning means that flooding is expected so you should act now. The Environment Agency suggests:

Move your loved ones, pets and valuables to a safe place.

Move to higher ground or the upper floor of a building.

Turn off the gas, electricity and water in your home if it's safe.

Put flood protection equipment in place.

Do as the emergency services tell you and help others if it's safe to do so.

Several flood alerts are in place including Christchurch Harbour due to high tides and also Preston Beach at Weymouth, Swanage Bay, Studland Bay, Sandbanks, Poole Harbour, Bournemouth Beach, Hengistbury Head.

Flood alerts on Dorset's west coast cover Lyme Regis, Charmouth, Seatown, West Bay, Bothenhampton, Burton Freshwater, Burton Bradstock, Cogden Beach, Chesil Beach, West Fleet, East Fleet.

The Met Office has issued a yellow weather warning for the south coast including Dorset, The Isle of Wight and Hampshire.

An amber weather warning for strong winds is in place for Cornwall and parts of Devon.

articles.title: Trump says Elon Musk restored Ukraine’s Starlink access but declines to say whether they spoke
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Thursday that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s Starlink access but declined to comment when asked whether he had spoken to the billionaire about the matter.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Thursday that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s Starlink access but declined to comment when asked whether he had spoken to the billionaire about the matter. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier Thursday that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starlink. “I don’t want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line — he put it back,” Trump told reporters when asked whether he spoke to Musk. Trump did not elaborate further. Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country’s attack and air defense drone missions against Russia. The Starlink system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after the Trump-Musk conversation, the Journal reported earlier, citing U.S. and Ukrainian officials. Some Ukrainian officials told the newspaper that the system had not been restored to full functionality but was working at higher speeds than under the cap. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier Thursday that speed on Starlink systems had not been restored for Ukraine, adding that he hoped for talks with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the coming days. Trump told Musk he was frustrated that the system’s speeds remained capped, according to the newspaper. Trump has denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown. Rubio told reporters Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Musk, not the White House. Zelenskyy’s relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy. Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones toward Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest U.S. push to end the conflict. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. Trump had promised to end the war when he took office, but the goal has remained elusive.
